string-array.name: municipalities_array
string-array.item: Beijing is the capital of China and the country\'s political, cultural and diplomatic centre. It lies in the north on a plain ringed by mountains, and it served as an imperial capital under several dynasties, including the Yuan, Ming and Qing. Landmarks such as the Forbidden City, the Temple of Heaven and the nearby Great Wall attract visitors from all over the world. The city hosted the 2008 and 2022 Olympic Games and is home to many of China\'s leading universities, government ministries and research institutes. Around twenty-one million people live in the municipality, which is divided into sixteen districts.

Shanghai is China\'s largest city and a global financial centre, built where the Yangtze River meets the East China Sea. Its history as a treaty port in the nineteenth century left an unusual mix of architecture, most visibly along the Bund, where old bank buildings face the towers of Pudong. The city is a major hub for shipping, manufacturing and finance, and its stock exchange ranks among the largest in the world. Shanghai also has a lively cultural scene, with museums, galleries and a famous film industry, and it hosted the World Expo in 2010.

Chongqing is a direct-administered municipality in south-west China, inland at the meeting point of the Yangtze and Jialing rivers. It became a municipality in 1997 and covers more land than the other three, taking in mountain villages and farmland as well as a crowded urban core. The city is an important industrial base and a transport hub for the upper Yangtze, and it is known for spicy hotpot, steep streets and misty weather. During the Second World War it served as China\'s wartime capital. More than thirty million people live here.

Tianjin is a direct-administered municipality on the coast of northern China, roughly 120 kilometres south-east of Beijing at the mouth of the Hai River. It grew into a major port and trading centre after it was opened to foreign trade in the nineteenth century, and parts of the city still keep the European-style buildings of that period. Today it is an important industrial and logistics city with a large artificial harbour and a free-trade zone, and it hosts a branch of the Chinese Academy of Sciences. Tianjin is also known for its snacks, crosstalk comedy and early modern schools.
